summary: Describes a transport model for SNMP that uses TLS or DTLS, providing authentication and privacy for network management messages. It defines how the TLS Transport Model implements the features of an SNMP transport subsystem. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The TLS Transport Model carries SNMP messages over TLS or DTLS. It checks certificates at both ends of a connection and passes the authenticated identity to SNMP access controls.

subtitle: How SNMP messages use TLS over TCP or DTLS over UDP with certificate-based identity checks.

tldr.problem: SNMP management messages need transport protection that can authenticate communicating entities and protect message contents.
tldr.mechanism: The TLS Transport Model carries SNMP over TLS/TCP or DTLS/UDP, uses X.509 certificates, and maps certificate identities to SNMP security names.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6353 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 5953 and has been updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 9456.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 6353 defines a transport model for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). It supports TLS over TCP and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) over UDP. Both modes use X.509 certificate-based authentication in this specification; other authentication methods are outside its scope.

The RFC also defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for configuring and monitoring the transport model. TLS may suit large transfers over a stream, while DTLS supports deployments that prefer a connectionless transport.
sections.plainLanguage: This document explains how SNMP messages can travel over TLS or DTLS. It also defines SNMP settings and counters for managing those secure connections.

sections.title: Where the Transport Model Fits
sections.content:
The TLS Transport Model (TLSTM) sits between the SNMP Message Dispatcher and the TLS or DTLS layer. For sending, it passes an SNMP message to TLS or DTLS for protection. For receiving, it takes a decrypted and integrity-checked message and passes it to the Dispatcher.

A TLSTM session is a secure association between two transport models and may carry multiple SNMP messages. The model keeps transport and security details in cached state, including the authenticated identity and a session identifier that remains unique and stable for that session.
sections.plainLanguage: TLSTM connects SNMP processing to TLS or DTLS. It protects outgoing messages and passes checked incoming messages back to SNMP.

sections.title: Certificates and SNMP Identity
sections.content:
TLSTM implementations are REQUIRED to support X.509 certificates. A connecting entity may use a certificate signed by a trusted Certificate Authority or a self-signed certificate. Trusted public keys must be installed through a trusted out-of-band process, and deployments SHOULD provide a way to check certificate revocation.

On the server, the client's certificate is mapped to a tmSecurityName using the certificate-to-name table. The mapping can use a subjectAltName, a CommonName, or a certificate fingerprint. The security model can then map that identity to the name used for SNMP access control.
sections.plainLanguage: Each endpoint presents a certificate, and the receiver checks it. The certificate is mapped to a name that SNMP access controls can use.

sections.title: Threats and Message Protection
sections.content:
TLS and DTLS protect message integrity and privacy, and help prevent impersonation and replay. Implementations MUST support authentication of both client and server and MUST support encryption against eavesdropping. DTLS uses sequence numbers and a sliding window for replay protection over UDP.

TLSTM MUST provide at least the security level requested by the SNMP application. A NULL integrity or encryption algorithm MUST NOT satisfy a request for authentication or privacy. DTLS cookies help limit some denial-of-service attacks based on spoofed addresses, but do not protect against attacks from valid addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The secure transport checks who is connected and whether messages changed in transit. For UDP connections, DTLS also checks for replayed messages.

sections.title: Opening, Using and Closing Sessions
sections.content:
When an outgoing message needs a session, TLSTM reuses a suitable open session or starts one. A client must check that the server certificate is the expected certificate and MUST NOT send SNMP messages until the server is authenticated and the connection is established. A server MUST request and authenticate the client's certificate before accepting SNMP messages.

For DTLS over UDP, each SNMP message MUST fit in one UDP datagram, though it may be split across DTLS records. The server MUST support DTLS cookies, and replay protection MUST be used. Closing a session MUST include a TLS close_notify alert.
sections.plainLanguage: Both endpoints verify certificates before exchanging SNMP messages. When the session ends, the closing endpoint sends a notice so the other side can clean up.

sections.title: Configuration and Transport Domains
sections.content:
The SNMP-TLS-TM-MIB defines counters, configuration tables, notifications, and text formats for addresses and certificate fingerprints. Its tables select client certificates, identify the server certificate to expect, and map incoming certificates to SNMP transport security names.

IANA assigned transport domain identifiers for TLS over TCP and DTLS over UDP. It also assigned port 10161 for command messages and port 10162 for notifications, for both TCP and UDP.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB provides settings for certificates and records session errors. The RFC also assigns transport identifiers and default ports for commands and notifications.
